# Iskra Belmonte

Iskra Belmonte serves as General Counsel at Thrace & Wexford, where she leads the legal
team responsible for the firm's cross-border contracts, dispute resolution, and regulatory
correspondence. Colleagues describe her as the person who reads every clause twice and
still catches something on the third pass — a habit that has made her the last signature
on nearly every agreement the firm's larger clients bring to the table. She is known
internally for restructuring the firm's contract review process so that flagged clauses
route directly to the relevant specialist rather than sitting in a shared inbox, a change
that cut the average review cycle nearly in half.

Before Thrace & Wexford, Belmonte was Deputy Counsel at Ornwell Maritime, where she worked
primarily on charter party disputes and cargo liability claims. It was there that she
first built the reputation that follows her now: a lawyer who would rather spend an extra
week narrowing a dispute to its actual point of disagreement than let it sprawl into a
multi-year arbitration. One of her former colleagues at Ornwell has said, half joking, that
Belmonte could find the one sentence in a hundred-page charter agreement that decided the
whole case, and usually did.

Belmonte also sits on the board of the Calloway Trust, a role she took on at the
recommendation of a former Ornwell client who had come to trust her judgment on matters far
outside shipping law. Her contributions there have leaned toward governance and conflicts
policy rather than the Trust's grant-making decisions, which she has said publicly is
deliberately outside her lane — she prefers to leave programmatic calls to people closer to
the communities the Trust serves. Even so, board members credit her with tightening the
Trust's conflict-of-interest disclosure process after she noticed a gap that had gone
unaddressed for years.

Earlier in her career, before either Ornwell or the Trust, Belmonte worked as a litigation
associate under Rutger Fennimore, a name still mentioned by people who trained under him
around that time. Fennimore was known for assigning associates cases well above their
formal experience level and then declining to intervene unless something was about to go
seriously wrong. Belmonte has credited that period with teaching her to trust her own
reading of a contract rather than deferring reflexively to precedent, a habit she says has
shaped nearly everything she has done since.

Outside her formal roles, Belmonte is a frequent mentor to younger lawyers moving from
litigation into in-house counsel work, a transition she has described as harder than it
looks from the outside because the skills that make someone a good litigator are not
automatically the skills that make someone a good business partner to the people they now
sit beside every day. She runs an informal reading group for junior counsel at
Thrace & Wexford, built around contract disputes she considers instructive rather than
famous, on the theory that the well-known cases have already been picked apart by everyone
else.

Those who have worked alongside her across her various roles tend to describe the same
thing in different words: that Belmonte treats a contract as something to be understood
rather than merely enforced, and that she is unusually willing to say when a client's
position is weaker than they think it is, even when a more agreeable answer would be
easier to deliver. That willingness has occasionally cost her a client relationship in the
short term, though colleagues say it has just as often been the reason a client came back
after taking her advice and finding it held up.
